extracted.intended_audience: children's librarians, authors, publishers, and general readers interested in children's literature awards
extracted.subtask_description: Standards, eligibility rules, and procedural practices used to choose the annual Newbery Medal winner and Honor Books (i.e., how books are judged, which books are eligible, and how the committee operates).

rubrics_metrics.name: Most distinguished contribution to American literature for children
rubrics_metrics.description: "The most distinguished contribution to American literature for children" (the phrasing used by the award).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the core evaluative standard: the medal is given annually to the author of the most distinguished contribution. The article repeatedly frames the award around literary distinction rather than popularity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Eligibility: author residency/citizenship and publication timing/language
rubrics_metrics.description: To be eligible, a book must be written by a United States citizen or resident and must be published first or simultaneously in the United States in English during the preceding year.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Medal is given to works published in English in the U.S. during the preceding year; the page also notes wording that the winner is the author of the most distinguished contribution "published by an American publisher in the United States in English during the preceding year."

rubrics_metrics.name: Selection committee composition and appointment
rubrics_metrics.description: The winner is selected at the ALA's Midwinter Conference by a fifteen-person committee; a new committee is formed every year, with "eight elected, six appointed, and one appointed Chair."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Committee members are chosen to represent a wide variety of libraries, teachers and book reviewers; composition and appointments are procedural requirements intended to produce a representative decision-making body.

rubrics_metrics.name: Selection process: reading, meetings, secrecy, and announcement
rubrics_metrics.description: Committee members read the books on their own time, then meet twice a year for closed discussions. The results of the committee vote are kept secret, and winners are notified by phone shortly before the award is announced. Newbery winners are announced at the Midwinter Meeting of the ALA.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Any qualifying book is eligible (does not have to be nominated). The process emphasizes closed deliberation, confidentiality of ballots, and timed public announcement at the ALA Midwinter Meeting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Honor Books must be subset of runners-up
rubrics_metrics.description: The Honor Books must be a subset of the runners-up on the final ballot, either the leading runners-up on that ballot or the leaders on one further ballot that excludes the winner.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Number of Honors varies historically (as few as zero and as many as eight historically); since 1938 the number of Honors or runners-up has typically been one to five. Honors are procedurally tied to the final-ballot results.

rubrics_metrics.name: Any qualifying book eligible (nominations unnecessary)
rubrics_metrics.description: Any book that qualifies is eligible; it does not have to have been nominated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historically books were nominated by librarians under earlier procedures, but current practice allows any qualifying work to be considered whether or not it was formally nominated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Emphasis on literary quality, not popularity
rubrics_metrics.description: "The criterion has never been popularity. It is about literary quality."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: ALSC leadership uses this language to distinguish the Newbery's evaluative focus; the page also records criticism that winners may be too difficult for children, reflecting tension between literary distinction and accessibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Award is literary and given to the author (not illustrator)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Newbery Medal is a literary award given to the author of the most distinguished contribution to American literature for children.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Newbery recognizes the text/authorial contribution; illustration is recognized by the separate Caldecott Medal. The article notes the medal is a literary (not illustration) prize and that winners receive a physical bronze medal engraved with their name.

rubrics_metrics.name: Joint authors are eligible
rubrics_metrics.description: Joint authors of a book were made explicitly eligible for the award (clarified in 1963).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This rule ensures coauthored works can receive the Medal; the clarification was added historically to remove ambiguity about eligibility for jointly authored books.

rubrics_metrics.name: Historical second-award unanimity rule (1932–1958)
rubrics_metrics.description: In 1932 a rule was made that an author would win a second Newbery only if the vote was unanimous; the rule was in place until 1958.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This historical rule was intended to encourage new writers by making repeat wins difficult; it is included in the article's history of changing selection rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Committee representativeness requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: Committee members are chosen to represent a wide variety of libraries, teachers and book reviewers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The representativeness requirement is procedural guidance intended to ensure multiple perspectives (school and public librarians, teachers, reviewers) inform the evaluation.
